choices: No — five-star reviews are always fake and should be discounted entirely
Yes — 95% is such a large majority that it must reflect true satisfaction

In Zeno's paradox, Achilles races a tortoise that gets a head start. Each time Achilles reaches the tortoise's last position, the tortoise has crept a bit further ahead — seemingly forever. In reality, does Achilles ever catch the tortoise?
choices: It depends on the tortoise's exact starting speed relative to Achilles
Yes — the infinite sequence of time intervals sums to a finite total, so he catches up in finite time
No — since there are infinitely many steps, it necessarily takes infinite time
No — Zeno proved motion itself is mathematically impossible

questions.q: You are shown two identical envelopes and told one contains exactly twice as much money as the other. You pick one at random and open it to find $100. You're offered the chance to switch. A tempting argument says: the other envelope holds either $50 or $200, each equally likely, so switching has an expected value of $125 — a gain over your $100. Is this switching argument correct?
choices: Yes, but only if you have no idea how much money might be in either envelope
Yes — you should always switch, since $125 expected value beats $100 for certain
No — you should never switch, because the first envelope you pick is always the larger one
No — the calculation invalidly treats $100 as fixed while the other side varies inconsistently; there is no rational reason to switch
